extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policy analysts conducting systematic reviews/meta-analyses or studying research integrity and survey methods
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review and meta-analysis of quantitative survey studies measuring how many researchers admit to or observe fabrication, falsification or data alteration; includes protocol-level inclusion/exclusion rules, data abstraction, statistical transformation, and meta-regression of methodological moderators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion: quantitative survey data on committing/observing misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Only quantitative survey data assessing how many researchers have committed or observed colleagues committing scientific misconduct in the past were included in this review. Surveys asking only opinions or perceptions about the frequency of misconduct were not included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only surveys that directly measure past occurrence (self- or non-self-reports) of relevant behaviours; exclude opinion/perception-only instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data format requirement: must provide frequency/percentage categories with a 'never' category
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies were included only if they presented data in frequency or percentage categories, one of which was a “never” or “none” or “nobody” category - indicating that the respondent had never committed or observed the behaviour in question. Studies lacking such a category, or presenting results in statistical formats that prevented the retrieval of this information (e.g. mean and standard deviation) were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To allow direct quantitative comparison, raw categorical counts/percentages with an explicit 'never' option are required; continuous summary statistics that preclude deriving a 'ever/never' count should be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents of any professional position and scientific discipline were included, as long as they were actively conducting publishable research, or directly involved in it (e.g. research administrators). Surveys addressing misconduct in undergraduate students were excluded, because it was unclear if the misconduct affected publishable scientific data or only scholastic results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict sample to individuals engaged in publishable research; do not mix in student-only samples whose misconduct may not affect the scientific record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral scope: include only actions that falsify or bias scientific knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: This review focused on all and only behaviours that can falsify or bias scientific knowledge through the unjustified alteration of data, results or their interpretation (e.g. any form of fabrication and falsification, intentional non-publication of results, biased methodology, misleading reporting, etc…). Plagiarism and professional misconduct (e.g. withholding information from colleagues, guest authorship, exploitation of subordinates etc...) were excluded from this review. Surveys that made no clear distinction between the former and latter types of misconduct (e.g. that asked about fabrication, falsification and plagiarism in the same question) were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and limit outcomes to behaviours that alter scientific knowledge; explicitly exclude plagiarism/professional-misconduct-only measures, and drop studies that conflate these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition principle: intention to deceive as key demarcation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimately, it is impossible to draw clear boundaries for scientific misconduct ... However, the intention to deceive is a key element. Unwilling errors or honest differences in designing or interpreting a research are currently not considered scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify incidents as misconduct only when there is an intention to deceive; treat honest error and honest interpretive differences as non-misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment and exclusion for meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys that did not sample respondents at random, or that did not provide sufficient information on the sampling methods employed where given a quality score of zero and excluded from the meta-analysis. All remaining papers were included, and were not graded on a quality scale, because the validity and use of quality measures in meta-analysis is controversial. Instead of using an arbitrary measure of quality, the actual effect of methodological characteristics on results was tested and then controlled for with regression analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective sampling-information criteria to exclude low-quality studies (non-random or undocumented sampling) from quantitative synthesis; avoid arbitrary composite quality scores and instead model methodological moderators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data abstraction: calculating 'ever' prevalence from categories
rubrics_metrics.description: For each question, the percentage of respondents who recalled committing or who observed (i.e. had direct knowledge of) a colleague who committed one or more times the specified behaviour was calculated. In the majority of cases, this required summing up the responses in all categories except the “none” or “never” category, and the “don't know” category. Some studies subdivided the sample ... In all these cases, the data was re-aggregated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract 'ever' counts by aggregating all affirmative categories; re-aggregate disaggregated demographic cells to produce study-level proportions when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main outcome metric: proportion recalling at least one incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The main outcome of the meta-analysis was the percentage (proportion) of respondents that recalled committing or that knew of a colleague committing the specified behaviour at least once in the given recall period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'ever at least once' proportion as the primary effect size for prevalence estimation; be explicit about recall periods when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple outcomes per study
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the biasing effect of multiple outcomes within the same study, all meta-analyses on the main outcome of interest (i.e. the prevalence of data fabrication, falsification and alteration) were conducted using only one outcome per study. For the same reason, in the regression analysis, which combined all available effect sizes on data fabrication, falsification and alteration, studies that had data both on self- and on non self- where used only for the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select one representative outcome per study for pooled analyses (pre-specified selection rule) to avoid within-study dependence; handle self- vs non-self-report overlap by predefining priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical transformation: logit transform proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: This measure was not normally distributed (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test: 0.240, df = 19, P = 0.005) so it was logit transformed, and weighted by inverse variance of logit transformed proportion using the following equations for effect size, standard error and weight, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply logit transformation to proportions to approximate normality before meta-analysis; compute weights by inverse variance on transformed scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pooling model and homogeneity testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean pooled effect size was calculated assuming a random effects model, and homogeneity was tested with Chochran's Q test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use random-effects pooling when between-study heterogeneity is expected; test for heterogeneity using Cochran's Q (and report I^2 where appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Between-group comparisons: inverse-variance weighted ANOVA
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between groups of studies were tested using inverse variance weighted one-way ANOVA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare subgroup pooled effects with inverse-variance weighted ANOVA to assess group differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression: model methodological and study characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The combined effect of independent variables on effect sizes was tested with inverse variance weighted regression assuming a random effects model and estimated via iterative maximum likelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meta-regression with appropriate weighting and REML/iterative ML estimation to test how study-level covariates explain heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate covariates and modeling strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The regression model first tested the combined effect of three methodological factors measured by binary variables (self- vs non-self- reports, handed vs mailed questionnaire, questions using the word “falsification” or “fabrication” vs questions using “alteration”, “modification” etc…). Then, the effect of several study characteristics was tested (year when the survey was conducted, surveys conducted in the USA vs anywhere else, surveys conducted exclusively on researchers vs any other, biomedical vs other types of research, social sciences vs natural sciences, medical consultants and practitioners vs other). To avoid over-fitting, each study characteristic was tested independently of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model core methodological moderators first, then test additional sample characteristics one-at-a-time to avoid overfitting given limited number of studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling diverse secondary outcomes (QRP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions on behaviours of secondary interest (questionable research practices) where too diverse to allow meaningful meta-analysis, so they were combined in broad categories for which only crude unweighted parameters were calculated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When items are heterogeneous and not comparable across studies, aggregate them into broader categories and report unweighted/crude summaries rather than pooled meta-analytic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias and sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular funnel-plot-based methods to test for publication bias in meta-analysis are inappropriate and potentially misleading when the number of included studies is small and heterogeneity is large. However, the robustness of results was assessed with a sensitivity analysis. Pooled weighted estimates for effect size and regression parameters were calculated leaving out one study at a time, and then compared to identify influential studies. In addition, to further assess the robustness of conclusions, meta-analyses and meta-regression were run without logit transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid funnel-plot-based bias tests with few heterogeneous studies; instead perform leave-one-out sensitivity analyses and compare results across analytic choices (e.g., transformed vs untransformed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct conservative estimate by excluding certain study types
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding all surveys that were not mailed, were not self-reports and that did not use the words “falsification” or “fabrication” yielded a maximally conservative pooled weighted estimate of 0.64% (N = 3, 95%CI: 0.25–1.63).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain conservative prevalence bounds, restrict analyses to study designs/methods hypothesized to minimize over-reporting (or, here, those yielding lower estimates) and report these sensitivity-based bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting prevalence metric limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of respondents that recall at least one incident of misconduct is a very rough measure of the frequency of misconduct, because some of the respondents might have committed several frauds, but others might have “sinned” only once. ... many of the included studies asked to recall at least one incident, so this limitation is intrinsic to large part of the raw data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly acknowledge limitations of 'ever' prevalence: it does not capture incident counts per person or the fraction of literature affected; discuss potential directions of bias (over- vs under-estimation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social desirability and reporting bias considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The accuracy of self-reports on scientific misconduct might be biased by the effect of social expectations. ... In the case of scientists, however, social expectations should always lead to underreporting, because a reputation of honesty and objectivity is fundamental in any stage of a scientific career. Anyone who has ever falsified research is probably unwilling to reveal it and/or to respond to the survey despite all guarantees of anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss likely underreporting in self-reports due to social desirability; consider design features (e.g., random-response technique) to mitigate such bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rule for study exclusion (non-distinct items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys that made no clear distinction between the former and latter types of misconduct (e.g. that asked about fabrication, falsification and plagiarism in the same question) were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude studies whose items conflate fundamentally different constructs (e.g., plagiarism vs data falsification) when the review targets only a specific behavior set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data extraction verification rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the objectivity of the information collected and the fact that all details affecting the quality of studies are reported in this paper, it was not necessary to have the data extracted/verified by more than one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and justify the data extraction verification approach; when study reports are clear and objective, single-extractor approaches may be acceptable but should be justified.
